subject: Intermittent on-prem GRE tunnel + ARP churn causing asymmetric flows / MSS issues
messages:
From: Eric Li <eric.li@netrix.com>

Cc: Netrix NOC <noc@netrix.com>
Date: Sun, 1 Aug 2027 09:18:00 -0700
Subject: GRE tunnel: intermittent reachability + MSS failure (attached pcap)

Hi Sofia,

We started seeing sporadic 502/connection reset errors to our private deployment this morning after a maintenance window. Short-lived connectivity blips every ~30-90s from a subset of ECS hosts. Troubleshooting on our side shows a lot of ARP churn and duplicated ARP replies on the customer edge for the GRE tunnel endpoint; we attached a short pcap.

Symptoms observed:
- TCP sessions frequently hit MSS/segmentation issues (MSS clamping seems inconsistent).
- Traffic for some clients is asymmetrically routed back out a different edge (same ASN) and is being dropped at our firewall due to state mismatch.
- BFD on the CE sometimes shows rapid flaps tied to the GRE interface.

We can provide a topology diagram and a quick capture (attached). Can you confirm if the on-prem agent / private node is publishing any route changes or ARP updates around the same timestamps?

Thanks,
Eric Li
Netrix Systems — Cloud Networking

Thanks Eric — I pulled the initial pcap and topology, and looping in Vivek and Marissa from infra/networking. Initial asks:

1) Can you confirm whether the GRE endpoint on the CE is doing proxy-arp for the customer subnet, or if you rely on layer-2 adjacency?
2) Do you see any CPU spikes or interface errors on the CE around the timestamps?
3) If possible, capture the BFD state transitions with timestamps.

Quick notes from our side: our on-prem private node (vpc-edge-nyc-3) has been reporting transient ARP table invalidations for the peer IP at 09:02/09:34/09:48 UTC (we correlate to your 09:xx logs after timezone conversion). We're concerned this is causing asymmetric return paths and stale conntrack entries on your firewall.

We'll triage options: MTU clamp to 1436 on the GRE, explicit proxy-ARP, and a short conntrack timeout bump during the investigation.

From: jonas_weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>

Date: Mon, 2 Aug 2027 08:27:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: GRE tunnel: intermittent reachability + MSS failure (attached pcap)

Adding analysis from the runtime/networking side. I pulled the pcap and the packet flow shows duplicated ARP "who-has" followed by two different hosts answering for the same /32 GRE endpoint — signs of flapping ARP proxies or an underlying VRRP failover oscillation. Specific observations:

- We see ICMP fragmentation-needed messages when packets exceed 1460 inner payload (GRE + outer headers push it above CE MTU).
- There are spikes of gratuitous ARP every ~60s.
- Our private node logs show route re-evaluations for the peer prefix at those timestamps, likely triggered by our internal health-check on the GRE interface (keepalive).

Immediate mitigations I'd propose:
- Apply MTU clamp on the GRE outer interface to 1436 (reduces fragmentation/PMTUD exposure).
- Temporarily disable BFD on the CE <-> Redwood GRE to see if BFD timers are causing flaps; if BFD is required, increase min-intervals.
- Enable proxy-arp only if CE is unable to resolve layer-2 for the customer subnet (avoid conflicting proxies).
- Short-term: bump conntrack timeout on Netrix firewall for ESTABLISHED to 300s while we stabilize.

I can push a canary config to the dedicated node during a scheduled 20-min window and monitor for ARP flaps. Thoughts?

Jonas Weber
Senior Network Engineer — Redwood Inference

Thanks Jonas — appreciate the analysis. A few follow-ups from our ops/security teams:

- We are hesitant to enable proxy-arp broadly because our firewall policy expects strict source validation; will consider proxy-arp only on the transit-facing interface.
- We can disable BFD for a test window; will coordinate with NOC.
- We'll approve a temporary conntrack ESTABLISHED timeout increase to 300s for the test window, but need Redwood to perform the canary during low traffic hours (we can do 02:00-02:30 UTC).

Also attaching a conntrack snapshot from our firewall showing a bunch of half-closed states at the problematic times — maybe that supports the stale state hypothesis.

Eric
